idiom_name: TableQuery[People] with filter/+=/update over a case-class projection
implementation_notes: Slick replaces the row object with a lifted table mapping: a Table[PersonRow] projection defines the columns, a TableQuery[People] is the typed handle, and CRUD is expressed as collection-like operations - people.filter(_.id === 1L).result.headOption, people += row, people.filter(_.id === 1L).map(_.deps).update(3). Rows are immutable case classes, so 'find, modify, save' becomes 'find, copy, update' and the gateway class disappears; keep the classic form only if you need mutable row objects, which Scala's ecosystem does not encourage.
pitfalls: The lifted embedding needs === instead of == and ++ instead of +, which silently differs from ordinary Scala semantics.
map(_.deps).update(3) requires an updatable projection; updating through a mapped case class needs a matching projection or it will not compile.
Every query returns a DBIOAction/Future that must be run on the right execution context; blocking JDBC work belongs on a dedicated pool.

variants.name: doobie sql"..." queries mapped to case classes in an effect system
variants.implementation_notes: doobie abandons the gateway object entirely: statements are written as the sql"..." interpolator with typed parameters, query[PersonRow].option maps a result row to a case class, and update.run performs writes - all composed as ConnectionIO values and discharged through a Transactor. Rows are immutable values and the finder is just a Query0 value, so the classic structure is replaced by SQL plus typeclass-driven mapping; this is the choice when the codebase is already built on cats-effect and referential transparency matters more than an object per row.
variants.code_sketch:
case class PersonRow(id: Long, lastName: String, deps: Int)

val findPerson = sql"select id, last_name, deps from people where id = $id"
  .query[PersonRow].option

val updateDeps = sql"update people set deps = $deps where id = $id".update.run

// findPerson(1L).transact(xa) : IO[Option[PersonRow]]
pitfalls: query[CaseClass] maps columns by position, so reordering the SELECT silently produces wrong field values.
JDBC is blocking: the transactor must use a bounded blocking execution context or it starves the effect runtime.
Nothing in doobie prevents running a write outside a transaction; wrap multi-statement work in a single transact.
